blocks.title: Original worked trace: prove a catalogue-release claim by resolution
blocks.problem: Premises: Checked implies Tagged; Tagged implies Ready; Checked. Query: Ready. Use propositional atoms C, T, R for this invented workflow.
steps: Eliminate implications: clauses are ¬C∨T, ¬T∨R, and C. These are premises in CNF, not an assertion that unchecked items cannot be ready.
Negate the query and add ¬R. Keep this temporary assumption separate from the original knowledge base.
Resolve C with ¬C∨T to derive T.
Resolve T with ¬T∨R to derive R.
Resolve R with ¬R to derive the empty clause. The negated query is inconsistent with these premises, so Ready is entailed.
Countermodel to the converse: C=false, T=true, R=true satisfies both implications and Ready, but not Checked. Without the original Checked premise, Ready would not entail Checked.
blocks.conclusion: The proof’s conclusion depends on its premises; it does not guarantee that a real item is safe to release. The clauses and countermodel are original.

chapters.title: Planning
chapters.summary: Choose actions whose preconditions and effects jointly achieve the goals, including the interactions between subgoals.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Choose actions whose preconditions and effects jointly achieve the goals, including the interactions between subgoals.

For this lesson: Define preconditions, add effects, and delete effects.

States

A planning problem describes initial and goal states and the available operators. The ebook uses preconditions and postconditions: what must hold before the action and what holds afterward. Classical planning also describes added and deleted facts as effects.

Operators

An action changes only part of the state. Specify its postconditions and keep track of unaffected facts. A convenient representation is not a license to ignore a condition that another action needs.

Partial Order Planning

Partial order planning leaves steps unordered until an ordering is needed. A causal link records a condition established for a later action. An action that could remove it creates a conflict that the plan must resolve.

Detecting Conflicts

Goals can interact. Achieving one may undo another, so solving each subgoal in isolation can fail. Check the whole sequence against the full goal state.

Hierarchical Task Network Planning

Hierarchical task network planning decomposes higher-level tasks into more specific tasks using domain knowledge. A decomposition still needs to fit the problem's constraints; a hierarchy does not make every resulting action sequence valid.

chapters.title: Understanding
chapters.summary: Understanding builds a structured interpretation of meaning, not just a parse of the words.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Understanding builds a structured interpretation of meaning, not just a parse of the words.

For this lesson: Fill thematic roles for an invented sentence.

Thematic Role Systems

Thematic role frames organize an event by roles such as agent, object, instrument, recipient, source, and destination. Roles describe participation in the event, not simply token positions.

Constraints

A verb can activate expectations about which roles should be filled and what types of entities can fill them. Observed words supply bottom-up evidence; the activated frame supplies top-down constraints.

Resolving Ambiguity in Prepositions

Ambiguity is resolved by comparing candidate interpretations against context and role constraints. The same word can have different meanings, and a syntactically acceptable reading can be semantically unsuitable.

Resolving Ambiguity in Verbs

Interpretation can remain uncertain. Do not claim that one frame removes every ambiguity or that the first noun is always the agent. Keep competing interpretations when evidence is insufficient.

chapters.title: Commonsense Reasoning
chapters.summary: Use structured background knowledge to connect meaning-equivalent actions and infer plausible consequences.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Use structured background knowledge to connect meaning-equivalent actions and infer plausible consequences.

For this lesson: Distinguish move-object, move-possession, and ingest.

Primitive Actions

The ebook calls its reusable action descriptions primitive actions. Move-object concerns physical movement, move-possession concerns a change in possession, and ingest concerns movement into the body. Propel, speak, and other primitives capture other kinds of action.

Thematic Roles and Primitive Actions

A primitive action has a frame with thematic roles and default expectations. Different verbs can activate the same primitive when their meaning fits; a single verb may need a different interpretation in another context.

Implied Actions

Commonsense reasoning uses context and background knowledge to interpret an action and infer what may follow. Separate the sentence's stated information from an inference supplied by the action model.

State Changes

Use the primitive action and its roles to describe implied actions and state changes. A physical movement need not transfer possession. Filling a frame does not prove that every expected consequence actually occurred.

chapters.title: Scripts
chapters.summary: A script encodes expectations about a recurring event sequence, including roles, entry conditions, scenes, and results.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
A script encodes expectations about a recurring event sequence, including roles, entry conditions, scenes, and results.

For this lesson: Specify a script's entry conditions, roles, props, scenes, and results.

Definition of Scripts

Scripts describe familiar, causally organized sequences. Their roles and props identify participants and objects; entry conditions establish when the script fits; scenes organize the progression; results describe expected outcomes.

Parts of a Script

Tracks represent variations of a familiar pattern. Context helps select and instantiate a suitable script rather than force every event into one universal sequence.

citations.section: Using a Script to Generate Expectations

blocks.text:
Using a Script to Generate Expectations

A script can fill gaps in a sparse story and predict what might happen next. Observed events activate the pattern, and the pattern supplies top-down expectations.

Tracks

Unexpected events may require a different track, goals-and-plans reasoning, or revision of the interpretation. Defaults can be culture- or situation-specific. Inferred scenes are not a historical audit trail of what actually happened.

chapters.title: Explanation-Based Learning
chapters.summary: Use prior domain knowledge to explain why an example works, then generalize the explanation's relevant structure.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Use prior domain knowledge to explain why an example works, then generalize the explanation's relevant structure.

For this lesson: Identify the domain theory used in an explanation.

Concept Space

Explanation-based learning can learn from a single explained example because it already has a domain theory. The example shows how to connect and operationalize knowledge, rather than supply all of it from scratch.

Prior Knowledge

Build an explanation for why the example satisfies the target concept or goal. Generalize the features and relations required by that explanation while discarding irrelevant specifics.

Abstraction

The learned rule can make future reasoning faster by compiling a multi-step explanation into a more direct procedure. Learning need not mean discovering an entirely new fact independent of prior knowledge.

Transfer

The result depends on the correctness and adequacy of the domain theory. A persuasive-sounding explanation is not enough; its steps must be justified. Contrast explanation-driven generalization with induction over many observations.

chapters.title: Analogical Reasoning
chapters.summary: Map relational structure from a known source to a target, transfer candidate knowledge, and evaluate whether it fits.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Map relational structure from a known source to a target, transfer candidate knowledge, and evaluate whether it fits.

For this lesson: Construct a role-preserving source-target mapping.

Process of Analogical Reasoning

The process includes retrieval, mapping, transfer, evaluation, and storage. A source may be chosen because it resembles the target, but mapping must establish a meaningful correspondence.

Three Types of Similarity

Superficial similarity concerns appearance; structural similarity concerns relations; pragmatic similarity concerns purpose or goals. They can point to different candidate sources.

Analogical Mapping

Structure mapping emphasizes relations and connected relational systems over incidental object attributes. A strong analogy aligns who plays which role in a shared pattern.

citations.section: Evaluation and Storage in Analogical Reasoning

blocks.text:
Evaluation and Storage in Analogical Reasoning

Transferred propositions are candidate inferences. Evaluate them in the target rather than assume that a good mapping makes every source property true. Design-by-analogy often transfers a useful mechanism while leaving material details behind.

chapters.title: Version Spaces
chapters.summary: Keep the hypotheses consistent with every labeled example, using general and specific boundaries instead of prematurely committing to one.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Keep the hypotheses consistent with every labeled example, using general and specific boundaries instead of prematurely committing to one.

For this lesson: Define a version space and its S/G boundaries.

Abstract Version Spaces

The ebook describes a specific model and a general model. A version space is the hypotheses in a chosen language consistent with the examples. The conventional S/G terminology describes the specific and general boundaries of that consistent set.

Visualizing Version Spaces

The boundaries can contain more than one hypothesis. Prune inconsistent and redundant candidates rather than commit prematurely. Generalizing the specific side and specializing the general side are complementary operations.

Version Spaces Algorithm

For a positive example, generalize an overly specific model and remove general hypotheses that reject it. For a negative example, specialize an overly general model and remove specific hypotheses that accept it. Both sides must stay consistent with the examples.

Identification Trees

An identification tree distinguishes instances using tests on their features. The ebook introduces this as another approach to classification and concept identification; it is not the S/G boundary representation of a version space.

Optimal Identification Trees

Under a fixed hypothesis space and faithful consistency updates, the final consistent set does not depend on example order. A single surviving hypothesis is not guaranteed: insufficient evidence can leave ambiguity, and contradictions or an inadequate language can leave no consistent hypothesis.

blocks.title: Preserved foundation explanation
items: The ebook describes a specific model and a general model. A version space is the hypotheses in a chosen language consistent with the examples. The conventional S/G terminology describes the specific and general boundaries of that consistent set.

For a positive example, generalize an overly specific model and remove general hypotheses that reject it. For a negative example, specialize an overly general model and remove specific hypotheses that accept it. Both sides must stay consistent with the examples.

The boundaries can contain more than one hypothesis. Prune inconsistent and redundant candidates rather than commit prematurely. Generalizing the specific side and specializing the general side are complementary operations.

Under a fixed hypothesis space and faithful consistency updates, the final consistent set does not depend on example order. A single surviving hypothesis is not guaranteed: insufficient evidence can leave ambiguity, and contradictions or an inadequate language can leave no consistent hypothesis.

chapters.title: Constraint Propagation
chapters.summary: Use local constraints to eliminate unsupported possibilities and propagate those eliminations, without assuming local consistency solves the whole problem.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Use local constraints to eliminate unsupported possibilities and propagate those eliminations, without assuming local consistency solves the whole problem.

For this lesson: Propagate a domain reduction through a small constraint graph.

Constraint Propagation Defined

A constraint problem identifies variables, possible values, and restrictions on combinations. Propagation uses one restriction to narrow domains elsewhere.

Line Labeling

In line labeling, junction constraints restrict how edge labels can meet. Revising a candidate label can affect neighboring junctions, so local changes propagate.

Constraints Intersections and Edges

If a domain becomes empty, the current assumptions are inconsistent. If no more values can be removed, the propagation procedure has reached a fixed point under its consistency rules.

More Complex Images

A nonempty fixed point may still contain multiple solutions or no global solution. Arc consistency requires local support along each binary constraint, not one joint assignment satisfying every constraint. Search or stronger reasoning may still be necessary.

blocks.title: Two colors on a triangle — step 1
blocks.problem: Three variables A, B, C each have {red, blue}; each pair must have different colors.
steps:
Check A-B: Each A value has an opposite supporting B value
The pair is locally supportable.
blocks.conclusion: The pair is locally supportable.

chapters.title: Configuration
chapters.summary: Select and arrange known components by assigning their variables so the complete set of constraints is satisfied.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Select and arrange known components by assigning their variables so the complete set of constraints is satisfied.

For this lesson: Distinguish routine configuration from open-ended design.

Define Design

Configuration is routine design: the component kinds and available choices are known, but their values, selection, or arrangement must be determined.

Defining Configuration

Represent components, variables, domains, and dependencies. Local compatibility is useful, but the final assignment must meet all stated goals and constraints.

The Configuration Process

A greedy assignment can become stuck even when another choice would work. Track dependencies and distinguish no solution under the current branch from no solution anywhere. An incomplete assignment is not a successful configuration.

Connection to Classification

Constraint propagation can narrow choices; classification can organize available components; case-based reasoning can supply a starting configuration. These are methods supporting the task, not synonyms for configuration.

blocks.title: A tiny catalog configuration — step 1
blocks.problem: Server options: small or large. Database: light or heavy. Constraint: heavy requires large. Goal: heavy database.

Set goal: Database=heavy
The goal fixes one variable.
blocks.conclusion: The goal fixes one variable.

The compatibility constraint removes small.

chapters.title: Diagnosis
chapters.summary: Explain unexpected observations by identifying fault hypotheses, while keeping explanatory plausibility distinct from proof.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Explain unexpected observations by identifying fault hypotheses, while keeping explanatory plausibility distinct from proof.

For this lesson: Separate data space from hypothesis space.

Defining Diagnosis

Diagnosis maps observations in data space to candidates in hypothesis space. It can be approached as classification or as abduction: infer an explanation that could account for the effects.

Data Space and Hypothesis Space

Data space contains observations; hypothesis space contains possible explanations. The mapping can be many-to-many. A hypothesis can also predict further observations, which can help distinguish competing explanations.

Deduction, Induction, Abduction

Deduction applies a rule and a cause to derive an effect. Abduction uses a rule and an observed effect to propose a cause. Induction learns a general relationship from observations. Reversing an implication is not a deductively valid rule.

Criteria for Choosing a Hypothesis

Coverage asks how much of the observed evidence a hypothesis set explains. Parsimony favors fewer or simpler faults under the model. Neither guarantees that the smallest explanation is the real cause.

Completing the Process

Multiple faults, competing explanations, and predicted-but-absent symptoms complicate diagnosis. Seek discriminating observations and keep the model's assumptions visible rather than force a single answer prematurely.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: A stipulated outage model — step 1
blocks.problem: Fault A explains latency and errors. Fault B explains latency. Fault C explains errors. Observed: latency and errors.
steps:
Generate hypotheses: {A} and {B,C}
Both explain the observed symptoms under this model.
blocks.conclusion: Both explain the observed symptoms under this model.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: A stipulated outage model — step 2
blocks.problem: Fault A explains latency and errors. Fault B explains latency. Fault C explains errors. Observed: latency and errors.
steps:
Compare coverage: Both cover latency and errors
Coverage alone does not distinguish them.
blocks.conclusion: Coverage alone does not distinguish them.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: A stipulated outage model — step 3
blocks.problem: Fault A explains latency and errors. Fault B explains latency. Fault C explains errors. Observed: latency and errors.
steps:
Compare parsimony: {A} uses one fault; {B,C} uses two
A preference for fewer faults favors A.
blocks.conclusion: A preference for fewer faults favors A.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: A stipulated outage model — step 4
blocks.problem: Fault A explains latency and errors. Fault B explains latency. Fault C explains errors. Observed: latency and errors.
steps:
Seek discriminating evidence: What else does A predict?
A new observation may reject the preferred explanation.
blocks.conclusion:
Parsimony ranks explanations; it does not logically establish the cause.
Fault effects are stipulated and simplified. Real diagnosis needs an adequate model and reliable observations.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: Your turn — original transfer exercise
blocks.text: Suppose A also predicts a missing signal that reliable monitoring says is absent. How should the diagnosis change?

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.title: Compare your explanation
blocks.text:
Under a deterministic model and reliable monitoring, the missing required effect counts against A. {B,C} may now be preferable despite being less parsimonious. If the effect is only typical or monitoring is incomplete, preserve uncertainty and seek more evidence.

Check your explanation:
Use the reliability and model assumptions explicitly.
Compare the contradiction with the alternative explanation.
Do not silently ignore the absent prediction.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.prompt: How do deduction and abduction differ?
blocks.answer: Deduction derives an effect from premises including a rule and cause. Abduction proposes a cause explaining an observed effect; it is not guaranteed by the effect alone.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.prompt: What are coverage and parsimony?
blocks.answer: Coverage measures explained observations; parsimony favors a smaller or simpler explanation under the model. They are selection criteria, not truth guarantees.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

blocks.prompt: Why consider absent symptoms?
blocks.answer: A hypothesis can explain observed symptoms while predicting something reliably known to be absent. That conflict can weaken or reject it under the model.

chapters.title: Learning by Correcting Mistakes
chapters.summary: Explain a failed expectation, assign blame to the responsible knowledge, and repair the mechanism rather than memorize the answer.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Explain a failed expectation, assign blame to the responsible knowledge, and repair the mechanism rather than memorize the answer.

For this lesson: Trace expectation, failure, blame, explanation, and repair.

Questions for Correcting Mistakes

An unexpected result creates a learning opportunity. Compare the prediction, actual result, and reasoning trace to identify where the expectation failed.

Error Detection Algorithm

Blame assignment locates the responsible knowledge or control choice: a bad case index, an invalid rule, an omitted condition, or an unsuitable strategy may be at fault.

Explaining the Mistake

An explanation supports a targeted repair. Change the part responsible for the failure, then evaluate the correction on the original case and related cases.

Correcting the Mistake

The agent must have mechanisms for the correction if you claim the agent learns. A human manually patching the implementation is not evidence that the system autonomously explains and repairs its own reasoning.

blocks.title: Repair a toy case index — step 1
blocks.problem: An agent retrieves incidents only by error text. A queue incident incorrectly retrieves a database-specific fix.
steps:

The failure must be explained.
blocks.conclusion: The failure must be explained.

blocks.conclusion:
The repair improves a general mechanism instead of attaching one output to one task ID.
The paper trace is an example of a possible correction, not proof that every retrieval error has this cause.

blocks.text:

Avoid changing every subsystem at once.

blocks.answer: Detect a violated expectation, assign blame, explain the failure, repair the responsible knowledge or reasoning, and evaluate the repair.

For this lesson: Separate object-level from meta-level decisions.

Beyond Mistakes Knowledge Gaps

A knowledge gap can lead to a learning goal. The agent seeks the missing connection or information needed to complete its reasoning. Goal-based autonomy can generate or revise goals in response to such gaps or failed expectations.

citations.section: The Blurred Line Between Cognition and Metacognition

blocks.text:
The Blurred Line Between Cognition and Metacognition

Cognition addresses the current task. Metacognition monitors and controls the reasoning and learning used to address it.

Strategy Selection

Strategy selection chooses a reasoning method using knowledge about the problem and the available methods. The choice should be justified by suitability, progress, or resource constraints, not by a fixed habit.

Strategy Integration

Strategy selection chooses a method; strategy integration combines methods. Use knowledge of the task, the methods, progress, and resource constraints to justify the decision.

Process of Meta-Reasoning

Meta-level reasoning can also use recorded experiences about earlier reasoning episodes. A controller needs a stop condition and a meaningful change in knowledge or strategy; repeating the same failed procedure is not improvement.

chapters.title: Advanced Topics
chapters.summary: Representation modality, creative processes, and ethical choices change what an agent can do and how we should evaluate it.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
Representation modality, creative processes, and ethical choices change what an agent can do and how we should evaluate it.

For this lesson: Compare symbolic and visuospatial affordances.

Two Views of Reasoning

Visuospatial reasoning operates on representations that preserve spatial structure. Symbolic representations explicitly describe objects and relations. The two views make different operations natural; an agent may combine them.

Symbol Grounding Problem

The symbol grounding problem asks how symbols acquire meaning connected to perception and the world. An image-like, or analogical, representation is a representation modality; analogical reasoning is the separate process of mapping knowledge from a source to a target.

Systems Thinking Connections

Systems thinking considers components, relationships, interactions, and levels of abstraction. A visible structure can depend on causal processes that are not directly visible.

Structure-Behavior-Function

Structure-Behavior-Function (SBF) models connect what a system is made of, how its processes produce behavior, and what the system is intended to accomplish. Models can be nested at different levels. These distinctions support diagnosis and design.

Agents Doing Design

Design constructs an artifact to meet requirements. Configuration is a routine design task using known components; more open-ended design may require other knowledge and methods.

Defining Creativity II

Creativity can be discussed through its outcomes and its processes. The ebook examines novelty and unexpectedness, and considers processes such as analogy. An unusual output alone is not a complete explanation of how it was produced.

AI Ethics

AI ethics considers the consequences and responsibilities associated with AI. The optional reading list expands this discussion and adds Semantic Web material, but its historical labels 28-31 are not additional current lessons.

chapters.title: Wrap-Up
chapters.summary: The course is a toolkit of representations, tasks, reasoning methods, learning mechanisms, and control strategies that can be composed.

blocks.title: Preview
blocks.text:
The course is a toolkit of representations, tasks, reasoning methods, learning mechanisms, and control strategies that can be composed.

For this lesson: Map methods and representations into a cognitive architecture.

Cognitive Systems Revisited

The cognitive architecture links perception, action, learning, memory, and reasoning. Meta-reasoning monitors and controls the process, including choosing and integrating strategies.

Course Structure Revisited

Group concepts by role rather than memorize them as an undifferentiated list. Semantic nets, frames, and scripts organize knowledge; classification, configuration, and diagnosis name tasks; reasoning and learning methods provide ways to perform and improve them.

Current Research

For an unfamiliar problem, identify the task, available knowledge, required relations, assumptions, and resource constraints before naming an algorithm. Explain why a chosen method fits and where it can fail.

Our Reflections

Reflect on your own agent with actual evidence. Keep submissions private under the course policy, preserve personal learning notes, and choose further reading from an unresolved question. Lesson 26 is outside the stated Exam 2 range of 13-25.

weeks.title: Adapt a case; do not just copy it

policies.title: Administrative source precedence
policies.text: Fall2026 syllabus and current official announcements override historical 2016 Raven assignments. Current linked assignment and exam instructions may change; these live pages were not independently reviewed. The supplied syllabus p.3 calendar is the authority for this pack’s Sunday dates.

policies.title: Deadlines are Anywhere on Earth
policies.text: The Fall2026 calendar states Sundays at 23:59 Anywhere on Earth (UTC−12). Stored timezone is the IANA identifier Etc/GMT+12, whose sign convention means UTC−12. The exported summary’s local display differs; do not read that display as an additional AoE deadline.

policies.title: AI supports learning, not assessed submissions
policies.text: Discussion with an AI learning assistant is allowed to develop understanding. Do not copy AI output into assessed documents or let AI generate assessed code or reports. Disable integrated assistance beyond a grammar checker in the assessed workspace. This original learning pack is not a homework-answer generator.

policies.title: Proctored exam content cannot leave the exam
policies.text: Do not seek live external input on exam material, use a second device, retain or share exam questions/screenshots, or transcribe actual questions into a tool that preserves access after the exam. This pack contains only original practice; it must not be used to store actual exam content.

policies.title: Original practice is diagnostic, not an official grade
policies.text: The 66 questions are original learning questions, not released course exams. Exact option-set agreement and decision-level feedback diagnose misconceptions; neither implements the official partial-credit algorithm nor predicts a course grade. The syllabus confirms partial credit but does not specify its formula.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

policies.title: Protect assessed work and verify submission
policies.text: Do not publish assessed code or actual submissions during or after the semester. Submit to the correct Canvas or Gradescope destination, then download and inspect the submitted file. Borrowed project-agnostic code needs clear attribution; course-project solutions and other students’ code cannot be copied.

policies.title: Fall2026 grade components
policies.text: Homework 15% (three at 5%); mini-projects 30% (five at 6%); ARC-AGI milestones 15% and final project 15%, with performance/report splits; exams 15% (two at 7.5%); participation 10%. These weights do not turn the pack’s original practice into assessed work.

practice.prompt: An agent interprets an alert, retrieves an earlier incident, adapts a proposal, and records its evaluated outcome. Which descriptions are justified?

options.text: Retrieving the incident is a role of memory.
options.explanation: Memory makes stored experience available to current reasoning.

options.text: Recording the evaluated outcome can support learning.
options.explanation: The experience changes what is available for future problems.

options.text: The representation of the alert can affect which incident is retrieved.
options.explanation: The representation determines which features and relations retrieval can use.

options.text: A correct answer proves that the agent uses the same mechanism as a human.
options.explanation: Equal outputs do not identify the process that generated them.

options.text: Learning, memory, and reasoning must run independently to count as a cognitive system.
options.explanation: Their interaction is central to the cognitive-systems perspective.

practice.explanation:
Correct: Memory makes stored experience available to current reasoning.
Correct: The experience changes what is available for future problems.
Correct: The representation determines which features and relations retrieval can use.
Incorrect: Equal outputs do not identify the process that generated them.
Incorrect: Their interaction is central to the cognitive-systems perspective.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: Consider the four views of AI and the knowledge-based perspective. Which statements are defensible?

options.text: Thinking and acting are one distinction; human-like and rational are another.
options.explanation: Crossing those two distinctions yields the four familiar views.

options.text: A rational agent is necessarily omniscient.
options.explanation: Rationality is not the same as complete information about the world.

options.text: KBAI is concerned with the relationship between computational agents and cognition.
options.explanation: The course studies cognitive systems and their knowledge-and-reasoning mechanisms.

options.text: An acting-oriented evaluation alone fully determines the agent's internal representation.
options.explanation: Behavior does not uniquely identify its underlying representation.

options.text: The knowledge-based perspective rules out any use of learning.
options.explanation: Learning is one of the course's fundamental interacting processes.

practice.explanation:
Correct: Crossing those two distinctions yields the four familiar views.
Incorrect: Rationality is not the same as complete information about the world.
Correct: The course studies cognitive systems and their knowledge-and-reasoning mechanisms.
Incorrect: Behavior does not uniquely identify its underlying representation.
Incorrect: Learning is one of the course's fundamental interacting processes.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: Two proposed agents return the same correct result on one problem. What can a mechanism-focused investigation reasonably do?

options.text: Inspect how each represents relevant relationships.
options.explanation: Representation is part of the proposed explanation of behavior.

options.text: Conclude that both generalize to every problem with the same answer.
options.explanation: One result is insufficient evidence of generalization.

options.text: Vary an incidental feature while preserving the relevant structure.
options.explanation: A controlled contrast probes what the mechanism relies on.

options.text: Ignore failure cases because the agents already succeeded once.
options.explanation: Failures help define the scope and limits of the proposed mechanism.

options.text: Compare the predicted behavior with observed behavior after a controlled change.
options.explanation: Predictions make the mechanism hypothesis testable.

practice.explanation:
Correct: Representation is part of the proposed explanation of behavior.
Incorrect: One result is insufficient evidence of generalization.
Correct: A controlled contrast probes what the mechanism relies on.
Incorrect: Failures help define the scope and limits of the proposed mechanism.
Correct: Predictions make the mechanism hypothesis testable.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: A learner builds an agent and uses a benchmark to study a cognitive hypothesis. Which claims stay within the evidence?

options.text: Implementing the hypothesis makes some of its assumptions explicit.
options.explanation: A working mechanism exposes representation and control decisions.

options.text: A benchmark score alone proves a complete theory of human cognition.
options.explanation: A bounded performance measure does not establish a complete cognitive theory.

options.text: A failed prediction can reveal a limitation in the proposed model.
options.explanation: The discrepancy can motivate revision or a narrower claim.

options.text: A memorized output and a structure-based solution are the same explanation.
options.explanation: The processes can differ despite returning the same output.

options.text: An agent experiment cannot teach anything unless it perfectly imitates a human.
options.explanation: A limited experiment can still test a bounded mechanism hypothesis.

practice.explanation:
Correct: A working mechanism exposes representation and control decisions.
Incorrect: A bounded performance measure does not establish a complete cognitive theory.
Correct: The discrepancy can motivate revision or a narrower claim.
Incorrect: The processes can differ despite returning the same output.
Incorrect: A limited experiment can still test a bounded mechanism hypothesis.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: What must be considered when treating a labeled graph as a semantic network?

options.text: The symbols that make up its lexicon.
options.explanation: The lexicon identifies the objects and relations available for representation.

options.text: The permitted structure and meaning of its relations.
options.explanation: Connections need an explicit interpretation, not just arrows.

options.text: Every directed edge automatically licenses its reverse.
options.explanation: Inverse or symmetric relations require appropriate semantics or rules.

options.text: Two graphs sharing their nodes can express different knowledge if their relations differ.
options.explanation: Edges, labels, and direction can differ while nodes remain unchanged.

options.text: A contains edge and an is-a edge can support different inferences.
options.explanation: Relation types have different semantics.

practice.explanation:
Correct: The lexicon identifies the objects and relations available for representation.
Correct: Connections need an explicit interpretation, not just arrows.
Incorrect: Inverse or symmetric relations require appropriate semantics or rules.
Correct: Edges, labels, and direction can differ while nodes remain unchanged.
Correct: Relation types have different semantics.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: A has DependsOn(api,db). B has DependsOn(db,api). C has DependsOn(worker,queue). Assume the A-to-B transformation reverses the dependency roles. Which follow?

options.text: A and B have different relational descriptions despite sharing their nodes.
options.explanation: The direction of dependence has changed.

options.text: The transformation can be represented as removing one relation and adding its reverse.
options.explanation: This is an explicit graph-edit description.

options.text: Applying the same role reversal to C yields DependsOn(queue,worker).
options.explanation: The source-to-target correspondence preserves the relational roles.

options.text: The transformation requires renaming worker to api.
options.explanation: Transfer concerns roles, not literal identity of node names.

options.text: DependsOn must be symmetric because both directions can be drawn.
options.explanation: Representability of an edge does not determine its semantic properties.

practice.explanation:
Correct: The direction of dependence has changed.
Correct: This is an explicit graph-edit description.
Correct: The source-to-target correspondence preserves the relational roles.
Incorrect: Transfer concerns roles, not literal identity of node names.
Incorrect: Representability of an edge does not determine its semantic properties.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: An associative semantic network uses spreading activation to help retrieve remembered concepts. Which statements are appropriate?

options.text: Activation can make connected concepts more accessible.
options.explanation: Spreading activation is a mechanism for associative retrieval.

options.text: An activated concept is thereby logically entailed by the original observation.
options.explanation: Association is not a proof of entailment.

options.text: Connection weights can affect which associations become prominent.
options.explanation: Weights can influence the retrieval process.

options.text: The strength of an association is necessarily a truth value.
options.explanation: Association strength and logical truth have different meanings.

options.text: Every activated memory is necessarily relevant to the current goal.
options.explanation: Associative retrieval can still return unsuitable knowledge.

practice.explanation:
Correct: Spreading activation is a mechanism for associative retrieval.
Incorrect: Association is not a proof of entailment.
Correct: Weights can influence the retrieval process.
Incorrect: Association strength and logical truth have different meanings.
Incorrect: Associative retrieval can still return unsuitable knowledge.

citations.section: Original teaching example, not source text or an assessed submission

practice.prompt: A scene representation records object colors but omits which object is inside which. The task depends on containment. Which conclusions are justified?

options.text: A more exhaustive search over the existing description necessarily recovers the omitted relation.
options.explanation: Search cannot generally recover information absent from the representation.

options.text: Adding containment relations may make the needed comparison expressible.
options.explanation: The new representation exposes a task-relevant distinction.

options.text: Every richer representation is automatically more efficient.
options.explanation: More detail can also add complexity and irrelevant distinctions.

options.text: Representation adequacy should be evaluated relative to the intended reasoning task.
options.explanation: What is useful depends on the operations and distinctions required.

options.text: Color equality is sufficient to prove containment equality.
options.explanation: The properties are independent in the stated task.

practice.explanation:
Incorrect: Search cannot generally recover information absent from the representation.

coverage.summary: Benchmark expansion covers Lessons01–12 with mechanisms, assumptions, original traces, transfer, vocabulary, and 12 original declarative diagrams. All 26 baseline lessons, 17 syllabus weeks, 66 current original questions, and 78 recall cards are preserved. Exact current practice and three historical answer-key revisions are stored independently of private inputs. Later lessons are foundation, not equivalently deep.

gaps.description: Lessons13–26 are preserved foundation, not full benchmark-depth reconstructions. Verified terminology corrections at pp.175, 202–205, 253, and 317 do not close this depth gap.

Linked readings remain bibliographic learning pointers. Full texts, editions, exact reading-page claims, and availability were not independently inspected; do not treat them as verified evidence for the new explanations.

Some preserved baseline guide heading/page pairings point to where a heading begins near a page boundary rather than where its substantive explanation appears (for example drop-link begins at p.123 and is explained at p.124). They are marked unverified; new mechanism blocks cite the inspected substantive ranges.

The ebook itself flags correspondence problems for Lessons02,04,14,25 and incomplete transcripts in Lessons03,05,24,25 on p.3. New explanations use inspectable PDF sections; video-link correspondence, precise timestamps, and missing transcript material were not verified or reconstructed.

Authenticated live Canvas pages, assignment rubrics, opening dates, and exam partial-credit formula were not independently reviewed. The supplied Fall2026 syllabus is the snapshot authority; current official announcements can supersede it.

The syllabus p.3 weekly table specifies Sunday 23:59 AoE; pp.7–9 render local summary times and the end-of-course survey differs from the week17 planning date. This pack uses the p.3 calendar for planning, flags the discrepancy, and makes no invented reconciliation of the survey deadline.

Lesson12 includes predicate/quantifier concepts and original scope counterexamples, but not a complete first-order resolution implementation, unification algorithm, Skolemization treatment, or exhaustive proof-search complexity account. The worked refutation is propositional.

provenance.method: Trusted baseline data evaluated with Node vm at conversion time only. New source-grounded explanations were authored after local PyMuPDF inspection of substantive ebook sections and the Fall2026 syllabus. Production consumes persistent validated JSON; no source PDF, transcript, private path, or input executable is required.
